source.title: Sparse is Enough in Fine-tuning Pre-trained Large Language Model
source.authors: Wei Song; Z. Li; Le-Fei Zhang; Hai Zhao; Bo Du

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports loss-landscape and gradient-distribution findings about pre-training and fine-tuning, but does not test random-label memorization, the listed generalization comparisons, or a measured relationship between a property and the training–test gap.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses generalization bounds and reports its own landscape and gradient measurements. Those results do not measure the training–test gap or test any listed version. Cited results from other work and downstream task performance comparisons are not included as claim rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures changes in language-model loss landscapes and gradient distributions after pre-training and evaluates sparse fine-tuning methods. It tests none of V1–V8. In particular, its landscape visualizations do not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its association with training–test gaps as required by V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors interpret pre-training as a prior shift that tightens a PAC-Bayesian bound, connect landscape and gradient differences to a compressed search space, and demonstrate competitive downstream adaptation through component-sparse SIFT updates. The tighter-bound interpretation is an argument, not a measured reduction in training–test gaps.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes pre-training and sparse downstream fine-tuning of language models; it does not use the original versions' random-label, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness-gap, or memorized-example interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The loss-landscape and gradient findings compare random initialization with pre-trained initialization. The fixed first-batch gradient component selection retains less gradient information for models trained from scratch than for pre-trained models; the text notes outlier samples but gives no numeric result for this comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: RoBERTa-base loss-landscape projections on GLUE show larger, sharper oscillations near pre-trained initialization than near random initialization; pre-training does not consistently lower initial task loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-training changes downstream-task loss-landscape geometry and has task-dependent effects on initial loss.

fits_no_version.finding: For the illustrated RoBERTa-Large parameter tensor on MNLI, the largest 1% of gradient components account for 99% of gradient norm, and the pre-trained maximum gradient is approximately two orders of magnitude larger than the scratch counterpart.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-trained language-model gradients can be highly concentrated in a small fraction of parameter components.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: The reported landscape comparison is qualitative and figure-based. The gradient results do not measure a training–test gap or establish that gradient concentration predicts one. The paper's GLUE and instruction-tuning results compare downstream task metrics, not the claim's generalization-gap outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No other results meet the row gate for the listed versions. The SIFT, random component selection, LoRA, adapter, and full fine-tuning task-performance comparisons evaluate downstream adaptation methods, not the specified generalization-gap claims. Figure 4's gradient-information comparison is described qualitatively but does not measure a listed version's outcome.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels using the same architecture and training recipe.
Network-width sweeps beyond zero training error and their effect on test error; varying the number of updated parameters in a fixed pre-trained model does not test this.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer held-out performance under limited or broader tuning.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce any penalty.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test gaps, and its ranking performance relative to norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Sharper oscillations at pre-trained initialization do not challenge V7: neither its sharpness measure nor its gap comparison is tested. The downstream fine-tuning comparisons and parameter-budget sweep are already declared in rows_left_out and do not supply missing tests of the listed versions.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and resulting test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image models.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization under different tuning regimes.
Large-batch versus small-batch generalization under fixed or adapted training budgets.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its relationship to the training–test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: RoBERTa-base
rows.stage_stated: random initialization and pre-trained initialization; downstream fine-tuning setup
rows.operation_detail: Compared one- and two-dimensional loss-landscape visualizations from random to pre-trained initialization.
rows.measure: Loss-landscape oscillation magnitude around the initializations.
rows.value: pre-trained initialization: high-amplitude, sharp oscillations; some tasks have higher loss near pre-trained initialization than near random initialization
rows.note: The text describes the figure's qualitative pattern and notes exceptions to the idea that pre-trained models always start at lower loss; no training–test gap is measured.
rows.check: The qualitative landscape result is reported, but cannot establish any listed version. Change observed to cannot_determine relative to the claims. The comparison concerns random and pre-trained initializations, rather than trained solutions with similarly low training loss.

rows.subject: RoBERTa-Large
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch and pre-trained; gradient measured on MNLI
rows.operation_detail: Measured the distribution and norm contribution of parameter gradients.
rows.measure: Share of total gradient norm represented by the top 1% of components.
rows.value: pre-trained: 1% of the components account for 99% of the total gradient norm
rows.note: This measures gradient concentration, not whether it tracks a training–test gap.
rows.check: The 1%-of-components/99%-of-gradient-norm result describes the illustrated parameter tensor in one RoBERTa-Large layer on MNLI; it is not a demonstrated whole-model aggregate. No listed version is measured.

rows.subject: RoBERTa-Large
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch and pre-trained; gradient measured on MNLI
rows.operation_detail: Compared gradient value ranges for one parameter's gradient distributions.
rows.baseline: trained from scratch: reference value range not stated
rows.value: pre-trained maximum is about two orders of magnitude higher than that from scratch
rows.note: The reported gradient-range difference is not related to a measured training–test gap.
rows.check: The approximately hundredfold maximum-gradient difference concerns the illustrated parameter tensor in one layer, rather than a demonstrated whole-model maximum. Gradient range does not measure any listed version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
